item.title: Developing and validating the human-AI collaboration competency scale
item.description:
Educational Technology Research and Development
Abstract Fostering learners’ capacity to collaborate effectively with AI has become an important goal in education. This study aims to develop and validate the Human–AI Collaboration Competency (HACC) Scale, which can be used to assess students’ perceived competency in allocating roles and managing tasks, and sharing, coordinating, and integrating with AI through ongoing interaction to achieve a common goal. This scale includes five constructs’’: engagement, fluency, team bond, interdependence, and task regulation. Two independent samples of high school students were used to examine the factor structures: Sample 1 (n = 195) was used for exploratory factor analysis (EFA), and Sample 2 (n = 356) was used for confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). The final version of the HACC Scale consisted of 25 items loaded onto 5 factors. Construct validity was supported through EFA and CFA, and evidence for convergent validity was obtained by examining the correlations between the measures of digital literacy, AI literacy, AI attitude, and collaborative learning skills. The findings provide empirical support for the internal structure and external associations of the HACC Scale, showing that this scale provides a basis for future research and instructional practices aimed at enhancing human–AI collaboration.

item.title: AI Self-Efficacy in Chinese Multilingual Learners’ Informal English Learning with Large Language Models: A Mixed-Methods Study
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
The rapid diffusion of large language models has made artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated informal digital learning of English (AI-IDLE) an emerging form of self-directed learning beyond formal classrooms. Although previous research has examined learners’ emotions and self-efficacy in AI-IDLE, less is known about how confidence in using AI relates to participation through emotions and ethical awareness specific to AI use. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study combined a cross-sectional survey of 1955 Chinese undergraduate English majors also studying an additional foreign language with interviews involving 30 respondents. Adapted five-point scales measured AI self-efficacy, enjoyment, boredom, ethical awareness, and AI-IDLE. Structural equation modeling identified a positive direct association between AI self-efficacy and AI-IDLE, alongside significant indirect associations through greater enjoyment, stronger ethical awareness, and lower boredom arising from AI use. Thematic analysis of the interviews contextualized these patterns through participants’ experiences of redirecting unsatisfactory exchanges, extending enjoyable practice, withdrawing from repetitive interactions, and setting boundaries around privacy and authorship. Drawing on quantitative and qualitative insights, this study identifies complementary affective and ethical-evaluative associations linking AI self-efficacy to AI-IDLE in an English-major sample with additional foreign-language learning experience. Learners’ accounts of evaluating AI assistance connect these participation patterns with the application of human intelligence.

item.title: Beyond affective coping and use frequency: academic rumination, generative AI dependency, and two dimensions of perceived cognitive debt
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support learning and emotion regulation, yet frequent or coping-oriented use does not necessarily constitute difficult-to-regulate dependency. It remains unclear how academic rumination and affective coping are positioned relative to dependency and whether dependency is differentially associated with perceived costs to knowledge internalization and independent reasoning. This study examined these distinctions within a single educational psychology model. Methods A cross-sectional survey included 611 current GenAI users recruited through university settings in Tianjin, China (91.7% first-year students). Dependency was a continuous, nonclinical tendency. Ordinal CFA and WLSMV SEM evaluated a prespecified partial association model. Covariate adjustment, four alternative measurement specifications, an AR-score hybrid, and observed-score regressions assessed sensitivity. Results In the reference model, academic rumination was associated with affective coping (β = 0.283), and both were associated with dependency (β = 0.187 and 0.555). Dependency was associated with perceived internalization/memory debt (β = 0.550) and independent-reasoning debt (β = 0.644); their standardized difference was 0.095 (95% Monte Carlo CI [0.032, 0.157]). The corresponding observed-score coefficients were 0.413 and 0.518, with a difference of 0.105 (95% bootstrap CI [0.035, 0.175]). Both serial coefficient products remained positive, but the negative conditional coping-internalization association was not sustained in the observed-score analysis. Reported frequency had no unique association in the combined adjusted model. Alternative measurement models retained robust RMSEA of 0.090–0.097; robust hybrid indices were unavailable. Conclusion The results provide tentative evidence of differentiated self-reported associations among coping, frequency, dependency, and cognitive concerns. Measurement misfit remains unresolved, and the coping-outcome coefficients were sensitive to construct representation. Observed-score consistency for dependency and serial products does not validate the latent structure or establish temporal or causal mediation. These predominantly first-year, Tianjin-based cross-sectional data do not establish objective cognitive decline or generality across student populations.

item.title: From technology to meaningful learning: cognitive, communicative, and cross-cultural effects of AI integration in bilingual education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in bilingual education is increasingly consequential for students' cognitive engagement and professional communication, yet prior research has examined these outcomes largely in isolation. Whether learning engagement and cross-cultural competence (CCC) operate as simultaneous, parallel indirect pathways linking AI integration to perceived learning effectiveness and business communication skill remains underexamined, and cultural intelligence has rarely been modeled as a boundary condition on the intercultural pathway. Methods Drawing on a cross-sectional dataset of 604 bilingual education students across 13 universities in China, this study integrated the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, Social Cognitive Theory, and Cultural Intelligence Theory within a single framework. Ordinary least squares regression with HC3 robust standard errors and partial least squares structural equation modeling with bootstrap-based indirect effect and latent moderation analyses were employed. Results All three indirect pathways were statistically supported: AI → learning engagement → perceived learning effectiveness (β = 0.191), AI → CCC → business communication skill (β = 0.278), and AI → CCC → perceived learning effectiveness (β = 0.202), each carrying a larger share of the AI-outcome association than the corresponding direct path. The model explained 28.38% of variance in learning engagement, 34.33% in CCC, 40.85% in business communication skill, and 47.28% in perceived learning effectiveness. Cultural intelligence positively moderated the AI → CCC association (β = 0.200), with simple slopes rising from 0.298 at low cultural intelligence to 0.697 at high cultural intelligence. Conclusion AI integration is associated with distal learning and communication outcomes predominantly through engagement-related and intercultural mechanisms, with cultural intelligence conditioning the strength of the intercultural pathway. These findings suggest that AI funding in bilingual education should be conditioned on process metrics, learning engagement and intercultural capability, rather than on tool procurement alone. Structured intercultural scaffolding should be required as an accreditation condition for AI-supported bilingual courses, and cultural intelligence screening at program entry with tiered support for lower-cultural-intelligence learners warrants consideration, given that the benefits of AI-supported learning are non-uniform across learners.

item.title: Code Craft: the digital design thinking and learning platform to enhance computational thinking and digital literacy
item.description:
Smart Learning Environments
Abstract This research develops an educational platform utilizing a design-thinking model to enhance computational thinking and digital literacy among undergraduate students in Thailand. The study was conducted in three phases: (1) investigating the learning experiences and needs of 400 learners and instructors; (2) designing and developing the integrated design-thinking model to improve computational thinking; and (3) deploying the platform and design-thinking learning model to enhance student computational thinking using 28 undergraduate students, evaluating its effectiveness and learner satisfaction. Quantitative analysis revealed that the platform significantly improved computational thinking mean scores at the 0.05 level, suggesting its potential as an effective learning tool. The prototype learning innovation comprises four key components: (1) fostering computational skills and digital literacy, with an emphasis on logical and algorithmic thinking, data handling, and software usage; (2) online assistance through the learning platform “Code Craft,” providing support and resources; (3) digital and artificial intelligence tools, facilitating interactive, modern learning experiences; and (4) enjoyment, ensuring an engaging and motivating learning process. The steps in this process are as follows: (1) discovering insights into learners’ needs and challenges; (2) tailoring the platform to user requirements; (3) generating ideas, encouraging creativity and innovative thinking; (4) prototyping solutions, developing practical applications and tools; and (5) testing and iteration, refining the platform from feedback and performance data. This approach illustrates the effectiveness of combining design-thinking instructional models and gamification in educational platform development, significantly improving computational thinking, preparing students for the labor market, and addressing the skills gap in technology and computational skills in higher education.

item.title: An Agent-Based Model of GenAI in Creative Writing: Novelty Gains and Diversity Declines
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is being rapidly adopted in education. Its effects on creativity unfold at both individual and collective levels. We develop an agent-based model that represents students’ creative outputs in a two-dimensional idea space to examine how GenAI assistance in creative writing shapes individual creativity and classroom-level idea diversity. Simulations show that GenAI increases individual creativity, with disproportionately larger gains for less creative students, while reducing collective diversity through idea homogenization. Critically, the model reveals a more nuanced, non-linear pattern of collective diversity than empirical accounts of homogenization alone: collective diversity can increase at low-to-moderate adoption rates before reaching a tipping point and declining at high adoption rates. These findings highlight the need to evaluate GenAI in education using both individual performance metrics and collective system outcomes.

item.title: The impact of feedback types on behavioral engagement: a machine learning analysis
item.description:
Interactive Learning Environments
Feedback is a critical component of the learning process, yet the consequences of performance-feedback granularity on adolescents remains unclear. This quasi-experimental study evaluated short-term differences in academic performance, psychological states, and behavioral engagement among 288 secondary students assigned to three conditions: Precise Ranking, Vague Grading, and No Feedback (control group). Data were triangulated using post-intervention academic performance, six achievement emotions, and computer-vision-derived behavioral engagement proxies. Adjusted academic performance was descriptively highest in the vague-grading condition compared with the precise-ranking and no-feedback conditions, although the overall condition effect was not statistically supported. At the individual level, anger and boredom were significantly associated with lower academic performance. Two descriptive patterns emerged in the temporal analysis of behavioral engagement: mean engagement increased after feedback in the precise-ranking condition, while the proportion of observations classified as constructive increased under vague grading. These findings suggest that feedback granularity may produce differentiated response profiles across learning dimensions. Because the feedback conditions were allocated to only six classes, the condition-level patterns should be considered preliminary. By integrating academic performance, achievement emotions, and temporally detailed behavioral indicators, this study demonstrates the value of evaluating classroom feedback as a multidimensional process.

item.title: Two Roads to Competence? How Cognitive and Affective Individual Differences Reach Applied Performance by Different Routes
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
Individual differences predict applied competence, but the routes by which they do so are rarely modelled. Drawing on investment and aptitude theory for cognitive resources and on appraisal theory for affective orientations, we propose an appraisal-correspondence principle: the closer an individual-difference variable stands to the outcome in its level of self-appraisal, the more directly it should act; the further away it is, the more mediation should be required. We tested the principle on pre-service teachers’ competence to teach with generative artificial intelligence (AI-TPACK), using a latent-variable model on cross-sectional data from 164 pre-service primary-school teachers in Türkiye. AI readiness (cognitive) and AI competence anxiety (affective) served as antecedents and generative AI literacy and AI self-efficacy as mediators. Fit was good, χ2(139) = 181.44, CFI = 0.978, TLI = 0.973, RMSEA = 0.045, and SRMR = 0.061, with 45.8% of AI-TPACK variance explained. Readiness produced a strong total effect (β = 0.600, 95% CI [0.444, 0.738]), half of it indirect; model comparison indicated that generative AI literacy, rather than self-efficacy, carries the mediated share, although the literacy → AI-TPACK path itself was only partially supported. Competence anxiety predicted neither mediator, and its direct path to AI-TPACK was small (β = −0.105, CI [−0.266, 0.059]) and not significant in any of 16 pre-specified data-handling variants. The cognitive road is robust; the affective road, as predicted by the principle, bypasses the mediators but leaves only a faint and uncertain trace. Full scalar invariance held across year of study and use frequency. We state the principle as a hypothesis for performance-based tests rather than as an established mechanism.

item.title: Assessing learning beyond AI assistance: assisted performance and unaided retention in generative AI-supported learning
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can improve task performance when support is available, yet these gains do not necessarily indicate what learners retain independently. This Mini Review examines three assessment conditions: assisted task performance, immediate testing without AI, and delayed testing without AI. Relevant evidence was identified through searches of the Web of Science Core Collection and supplementary source identification. Across the reviewed experiments, outcomes varied with task demands, instructional design and the skills assessed. Unrestricted AI assistance was associated with weaker subsequent performance in some comparisons, whereas structured AI-supported instruction showed benefits for selected outcomes. None of the twelve selected studies documented all three conditions with verified AI exclusion at both no-AI posttests. Variation in baseline measurement, follow-up intervals and instructional comparators further limits cross-study interpretation. Retrieval attempts, elaboration and feedback use offer plausible explanations, but their roles as mediators remain largely untested. Future studies should document AI availability during learning and testing, specify the constructs assessed, and report learning activities between assessments.

item.title: Information overload, cognitive fatigue, and postgraduates’ intention to use generative artificial intelligence for English academic writing: the role of lower-order cognitive offloading
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) returns large amounts of information that postgraduates must judge and integrate when they write in English. The stressor-strain-outcome framework suggests that such overload strains cognitive resources and weakens plans for further use. This study tested whether cognitive fatigue links perceived information overload with later behavioral intention to use AI for English academic writing. It also tested whether lower-order cognitive offloading, such as having AI summarize papers, conditions the overload-fatigue association. Methods In total, 475 Chinese master’s and doctoral students who used AI for English academic writing completed three surveys at two-week intervals. Overload and offloading were measured at Time 1, fatigue at Time 2, and intention at Time 3. A moderated mediation model adjusted for baseline fatigue, baseline intention, and AI-use frequency. Results Higher perceived information overload accompanied higher cognitive fatigue 2 weeks later and weaker behavioral intention 4 weeks later, net of baseline levels. Cognitive fatigue was associated with weaker later intention and carried part of the overload-intention association. The overload-fatigue association was weaker at higher levels of lower-order cognitive offloading. Among the most frequent offloaders it was not statistically significant, which does not indicate its absence. The indirect association through fatigue was likewise weaker at higher offloading. These patterns held with additional covariates, a competing interaction with AI-use frequency, and shortened scales. Conclusion In this sample, cognitive fatigue accompanied the prospective association between overload and weaker plans to use AI. This pathway was weaker among postgraduates who delegated foundational tasks more often. Writing programs can teach students which foundational tasks to delegate, and tool developers can limit output overload.

item.title: Generative AI feedback use and deep cognitive engagement in university EFL writing: a mixed-methods study of autonomy, self-regulated learning, and AI literacy
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to obtain feedback in English as a foreign language (EFL) writing, but its educational significance depends on how learners interpret and regulate that feedback. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory and self-regulated learning theory, this explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examined an AI-supported motivated self-regulated learning framework using a cross-sectional survey of 486 university EFL students and follow-up interviews with 20 students. Structural equation modeling identified a positive direct association between reported AI feedback use and deep cognitive engagement, together with a positive indirect statistical association through learning autonomy and self-regulated learning. The AI feedback use–autonomy association was stronger at higher modeled levels of AI literacy. Interview accounts described feedback-related control, critical evaluation, and awareness of AI limitations, alongside contrasting experiences of rapid polishing and careful evaluation despite limited familiarity with AI. Integration of the two strands highlighted variation in how learners evaluated and incorporated feedback. These self-report findings do not establish temporal ordering or causal effects. They identify learner agency, strategic regulation, and critical evaluation as relevant considerations for future investigations of AI-supported writing.

item.title: Effects of structured generative AI feedback on data science students' critical thinking: a propensity score matching approach
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background AI feedback holds promise for supporting student learning, but unstructured use can lead students to passively accept AI-generated answers, weakening their independent reasoning. This study examined whether structured AI feedback affects undergraduate students' critical thinking, learning performance, and engagement in a data science analytics course. Methods An exploratory two-class quasi-experimental study was conducted in a three-month undergraduate data science course ( N = 167). One class received four-phase structured AI feedback, while the comparison class received conventional instructor feedback. Propensity score matching was used to improve comparability on observed baseline characteristics. Critical thinking was assessed using an adapted 40-item assessment covering five dimensions. Results Students receiving structured AI feedback demonstrated higher post-test critical thinking scores than matched controls, with a baseline-adjusted difference of 5.64 points (95% CI [3.62, 7.65], p < 0.001). A significant between-group difference in pre-to-post changes was also observed. Dimension-level analyses revealed significant differences in Evaluation of Arguments, Interpretation, Recognition of Assumptions, and Inference, while Deduction showed no significant difference. Higher learning performance, cognitive engagement, and behavioral engagement were also observed in the structured AI feedback group, whereas emotional engagement did not differ significantly between groups. Conclusion The findings provide exploratory evidence of differences in critical thinking and learning outcomes between the structured AI feedback and conventional instructor feedback classes. They highlight the potential relevance of feedback designs that encourage students to actively evaluate, question, and revise AI-supported analytical work, while underscoring the need for further studies that can isolate intervention-specific effects.

item.title: From web-based interaction to generative AI: two decades of research in Interactive Learning Environments (2006–2025)
item.description:
Interactive Learning Environments
Interactive learning environments encompass web-based collaboration, mobile and immersive media, adaptive systems, and generative artificial intelligence. This study examines how the research published in Interactive Learning Environments changed across two complete decades. Scopus-indexed articles and reviews were analysed using longitudinal bibliometrics, keyword co-occurrence, reference co-citation, and source-aware metadata coding. Publication growth coincided with expanding attention to immersive and AI-mediated interaction. A common distributional measure indicated greater redistribution among coded technology categories than among pedagogical categories, including in sensitivity analyses restricted by keyword availability and abstract length. These results concern metadata-visible research emphases and do not establish different rates of change in educational practice. AI-family research increasingly foregrounded dialogue, while the growth of content generation was concentrated in the generative-AI subset. Nonsignificant comparisons across other dimensions did not establish equivalence. We interpret these patterns through cumulative reconfiguration, defined as the coexistence of established research concerns with changes in the functions assigned to technological systems. This interpretation remains bounded by the journal-specific corpus, unequal metadata reporting, and the absence of independent full-text coding.

item.title: Generative operationalism: when LLM-based item generation displaces construct theory in educational and psychological measurement
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly changing automated item generation (AIG) by enabling researchers to produce extensive pools of educational and psychological items with little time and human labor. Although this development is usually discussed as a technical improvement in test construction, it raises a more fundamental philosophical question: What warrants the claim that a machine-generated item measures the attribute assigned to it? This paper introduces the concept of generative operationalism to describe a mode of test development in which an ordinary-language construct label is supplied to a generative model, its outputs are treated as operationalizations of that construct, and post-hoc psychometric regularities are subsequently interpreted as evidence that the construct has been successfully measured. Drawing primarily on causal realism, we argue that LLM-generated items are not necessarily invalid for measuring their target attributes, but rather, theory-displacing uses of AIG weaken the epistemic warrant for the proposed causal pathway from the target attribute to the observed response. They may also produce semantic redundancy, construct underrepresentation, method variance, and residual dependence that generate apparently desirable psychometric properties without establishing that the intended attribute causally influences responses. The central problem is therefore not machine authorship itself, but the substitution of linguistic plausibility and statistical regularity for an independently articulated theory of the construct and its response processes. We conclude by specifying conditions under which LLMs can function as theory-implementing instruments rather than engines of generative operationalism .

item.title: From cognitive relief to motivational enhancement: associations between perceived Agentic AI Capability and student engagement in systems development courses
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative AI agents are increasingly emerging as important learning partners for supporting complex problem-solving in higher education; however, the psychological processes associated with student engagement remain insufficiently understood. Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines how perceived Agentic AI Capability is associated with students' extraneous cognitive load, academic self-efficacy, and overall student engagement in systems development courses. An empirical study was conducted among undergraduate students majoring in e-commerce who participated in systems development-related courses. The results indicate that perceived Agentic AI Capability is negatively associated with extraneous cognitive load and positively associated with academic self-efficacy. Extraneous cognitive load is negatively associated with academic self-efficacy and student engagement, whereas academic self-efficacy is positively associated with student engagement. The indirect associations through academic self-efficacy and the sequential pathway are statistically significant. The findings provide evidence on cognitive and motivational correlates of AI-supported learning while, given the cross-sectional design, not establishing causal or temporal relationships. This study extends the application of Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory to human–AI collaborative learning environments and provides theoretical insights and practical implications for integrating generative AI into systems development education.

item.title: Human–machine collaborative literacy and tourism SMEs’ perceived digital transformation performance: a configurational fsQCA
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes embedded in tourism service work, employees increasingly need to interpret machine-generated outputs, evaluate their usefulness, and integrate them into organisational activities. Yet little is known about the firm-level resource configurations in which workforce human–machine collaborative literacy (HC) accompanies favourable digital transformation performance. Integrating organisational psychology perspectives on human–AI work with the technology–organisation–environment framework and a digital eco-embedding perspective, this study applied fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to 401 managerial questionnaires aggregated to 30 Chinese tourism small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). The analysis examined manager-perceived workforce HC alongside intelligent technology infrastructure (TI), digital niche (IO), policy support (PS), and open innovation networks (CN). No individual condition or its negation was necessary for high perceived performance (HC necessity consistency = 0.845). Two high-performance configurations shared core TI and IO: H1 included peripheral CN, with HC unspecified, whereas H2 included peripheral HC and PS. Seven firms satisfied the descriptive membership criterion for both high-performance configurations. Three non-high-performance configurations shared the absence of digital niche (~IO), with the absence of HC specified in two. The intermediate expressions were retained across the examined calibration and truth-table threshold settings. In the leave-one-firm-out analyses, the complete high-performance intermediate solution was retained in 28 of 30 deletions and the H2 conjunction in all 30, whereas the complete non-high-performance intermediate solution was retained in 20 of 30 deletions. These findings position manager-perceived workforce HC as a configuration-specific complement rather than a universally necessary condition for favourable perceived transformation performance. By situating a workforce-related capability within technological, ecosystem, and institutional resource configurations, the study provides an organisational-level contextual perspective on human–AI collaboration. The findings suggest that workforce capability development should be considered alongside technological readiness, digital ecosystem access, and institutional support.

item.title: Artificial intelligence readiness and innovative work behavior among university engineering teachers: parallel indirect effects of creative self-efficacy and technology integration self-efficacy
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming part of university teachers’ teaching and research, yet its relationship with innovative work behavior in engineering education remains unclear. Methods Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory and Conservation of Resources Theory, this cross-sectional study surveyed 786 university engineering teachers in Chongqing, China. We examined the association between AI readiness and innovative work behavior and tested parallel indirect effects through creative self-efficacy and technology integration self-efficacy. Gender and educational attainment were included as covariates. Results AI readiness was positively associated with innovative work behavior. The indirect paths through creative self-efficacy and technology integration self-efficacy were both significant. AI readiness remained significantly associated with innovative work behavior after both mediators were included, indicating partial mediation. Discussion These findings suggest that AI readiness and efficacy beliefs may support innovative work among engineering teachers. Universities can support quality education by linking AI training to course design, laboratory teaching, project development, and research tasks, while using guided practice and feedback to build teachers’ confidence.

item.title: Teaching while researching in a smart classroom: community-engaged action research on microlecturing for teachers’ professional learning
item.description:
Smart Learning Environments
Abstract The widespread digital technologies, including artificial intelligence, have largely elevated student experiences and achievements in higher education, but the simultaneous upgrade of teacher capacity, particularly the resources and opportunities for teachers’ professional development in everyday class, were less attended. To investigate how a smart classroom can be orchestrated to boost teachers’ self-exploration and collaboration in digital teaching, this study employed the technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK) framework to probe how teachers advanced their professional learning through design, implementation, and revision of VoiceThread microlectures for students’ Chinese character learning outside the class. Collaborative action research was conducted over four years to create a teaching community comprising the researcher and five teachers to enhance contextual smartness, that is, digital technologies and teachers’ context-aware, adaptive, and personalized use of them, in Chinese language classrooms. Semi-structured teacher interviews, community discussion, and surveys from 227 students showed that teachers utilized microlecturing to strengthen their TPACK about Chinese characters alongside class progress. This TPACKing process not just promoted research-practice dialogues but reinforced teachers’ beliefs and strategies to carry out professional learning in smart classrooms. The findings suggested a dynamic re-framing of TPACK with means of updating and interacting with contexts, content, technologies, and pedagogies in smart learning environments. The study also offered tips to keep up language teachers’ continuing professional development in daily instruction.

item.title: Human and AI Judgment in EFL Speaking Assessment: Psychometric Dependability, Feedback Quantity and Coverage, and Exploratory Teacher Perspectives
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
This study examined human-AI judgment in EFL speaking assessment as a measurement problem relevant to research on individual differences: how consistently do expert raters and repeated AI sessions preserve between-person differences in a complex performance? Thirty oral-performance samples from first-year Chinese university English majors were evaluated by four experienced EFL teachers and by ChatGPT-4o across four repeated sessions using the same holistic and accuracy-fluency-complexity framework. Score distributions were summarized descriptively; human-rater intraclass correlations and generalizability-theory G- and D-studies evaluated dependability. Feedback quantity and thematic coverage were summarized descriptively, and post-results interviews with the same four teacher-raters were analyzed as exploratory participant reflections. Teachers produced more dependable single ratings. Holistic phi coefficients were 0.54 for one ChatGPT-4o session and 0.65 for one teacher, increasing to 0.83 and 0.88 with four assessments. Analytic single-assessment coefficients ranged from 0.54 to 0.56 for ChatGPT-4o and 0.61 to 0.65 for teachers. Across holistic and analytic scoring, a phi coefficient of at least 0.80 was reached with four repeated ChatGPT-4o sessions but three independent teachers. ChatGPT-4o’s analytic dimensions showed limited differentiation from its holistic scoring: accuracy matched the holistic score in all 120 AI ratings, while fluency and complexity differed in only three and four ratings, respectively. ChatGPT-4o also produced more rubric-relevant comments descriptively, while the four teacher-raters emphasized human oversight for contextual and interpersonal interpretation. The study contributes to intelligence research at the level of psychometric measurement and human-AI judgment: assessor systems can differentially preserve observed individual differences in complex performance. EFL speaking was not treated as an intelligence test, and unmeasured cognitive mechanisms were not inferred from the score patterns.

item.title: Generative AI use and scientific literacy among 15-year-olds in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, China: the mediating role of academic help-seeking
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Adolescents increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots for schoolwork, yet evidence on whether this use supports or undermines learning is mixed. Drawing on research on cognitive offloading and self-regulated learning, we examined whether GenAI use for schoolwork is related to scientific literacy directly and through two components of self-regulated learning, academic help-seeking and metacognitive strategy use, and whether the purpose of use matters. Methods We analyzed the Program for International Student Assessment 2025 (PISA 2025) data from 12,191 15-year-old students in 374 schools in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, China. Weighted two-level mediation models compared students within the same school, used all ten plausible values, and evaluated indirect effects with Monte Carlo confidence intervals. Results were checked against a design-based model with school fixed effects and balanced repeated replication weights. Results Students who used GenAI more often than their schoolmates reported more help-seeking ( β = 0.17) and more metacognitive strategy use ( β = 0.30). Help-seeking was positively associated with scientific literacy, yielding a positive indirect effect ( β = 0.013, 95% CI [0.009, 0.017]); the indirect effect through metacognitive strategies was smaller ( β = 0.007) and was fully accounted for by science self-efficacy. The direct association between GenAI use and scientific literacy was negative ( β = −0.048, about 4 PISA points), and the positive indirect effects offset about 40% of it, leaving a small negative total association ( β = −0.028). Purpose mattered: among users, using GenAI “to help me learn” was associated with higher scientific literacy (+5.8 points per response category), whereas using it to summarize texts, research new topics, or draft assignments was associated with lower scores (−6.6 points). The results did not differ by gender or socioeconomic status and were identical under the design-based model. Discussion GenAI use for schoolwork is associated with scientific literacy through opposing pathways: a positive one through academic help-seeking and a negative direct one, and the direction of the association differs by purpose of use. Because the data are cross-sectional, these associations may partly reflect which students use GenAI rather than the effects of its use.

item.title: The relationship between attitudes toward artificial intelligence and digital literacy skills: a sports sciences perspective
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI)-supported applications in sports sciences, such as performance analysis, injury risk prediction, and data-driven training, underscores the importance of understanding the link between students’ digital competencies and their perceptions of AI. This study examined the relationship between sports science students’ attitudes toward AI and their levels of digital literacy. Methods A correlational survey design was used. The sample consisted of 229 female and 314 male undergraduate students ( n = 543; Mage = 21.16, SD = 4.5) from 13 state and foundation universities across Türkiye. Data were collected through a demographic information form, the Digital Literacy Scale, and the General Attitudes Toward Artificial Intelligence Scale. Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics 25, JASP 0.19.3.0, AMOS 24, and Minitab 20. Confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling were used to test the relationships among variables. Results Positive attitudes toward AI were significantly and positively associated with digital literacy ( β = 0.55, p < 0.001), whereas negative attitudes showed a weaker but significant negative association ( β = −0.20, p < 0.001). The model explained 38.4% of the variance in digital literacy ( R 2 = 0.384). Discussion These results suggest that positive AI perceptions may support students’ engagement with digital environments, whereas negative perceptions may constrain it. The study emphasizes the importance of educational experiences that enhance AI awareness and strengthen digital literacy within sports science programs.

item.title: Label or not: AI-generated news labels and perceived credibility among Chinese readers
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Artificial intelligence increasingly writes the news, and Chinese regulation has required explicit labels on AI-generated content since September 2025, yet what such labels do to readers’ trust remains an open question. This experiment tested whether an AI-generated news label changes perceived credibility, whether perceived human involvement explains the change, and whether readers’ AI literacy conditions it. Methods A sample of 1,024 Chinese adults (51.7% female; mean age 30.8 years) recruited through an online panel was randomly assigned to read one of two news stories that either carried a prominent AI-generated label or carried no authorship label, in a 2 (label: AI-generated vs. no label) × 2 (news topic: health technology vs. urban culture) between-subjects design with 256 per cell. Participants rated perceived human involvement, message credibility, and their own AI literacy. Results The label lowered perceived credibility (β = −0.31, p < 0.001) and perceived human involvement ( F (1, 1,020) = 218.60, p < 0.001). Involvement mediated the label effect on credibility: the indirect effect was β = −0.19, 95% CI [−0.23, −0.16], about three fifths of the total effect. AI literacy moderated the label-to-involvement path (β = 0.10, p < 0.001): the label penalty was β = −0.52 at low literacy and β = −0.32 at high literacy, and the index of moderated mediation was β = 0.05, 95% CI [0.02, 0.08]. Discussion The credibility cost of AI news labels travels through perceived human involvement and concentrates among readers with little AI literacy. Labeling regimes can keep AI-generated news transparent without flatlining trust, but they work best alongside AI literacy education.

item.title: Perceived career impacts of artificial intelligence and career decision-making self-efficacy among Chinese college students: the mediating roles of career planning and career anxiety
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping labor market structures and transforming how college students perceive their future career development. Understanding the psychological processes associated with the relationships between perceptions of AI and career-related outcomes has therefore become increasingly important. Drawing on Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT), this study examined the relationships between perceived career impacts of AI and career decision-making self-efficacy among college students, with particular attention to the indirect roles of career planning and career anxiety. A questionnaire survey was conducted with 415 Chinese college students, and the proposed hypotheses were tested using structural equation modeling. The results showed that positive perceived career impacts of AI were positively associated with career decision-making self-efficacy, with career planning representing an indirect pathway in this relationship. In contrast, negative perceived career impacts of AI were not directly associated with career decision-making self-efficacy but were indirectly associated with lower self-efficacy through an indirect association involving career anxiety. These findings indicate that college students' perceptions of AI are associated with career decision-making self-efficacy through distinct cognitive and affective processes. The study provides empirical support for the applicability of SCCT in understanding career development in the context of AI and enriches the literature on the relationships between AI-related career perceptions and students' career decision-making processes.
